summary: OWAMP and TWAMP measure delay using timestamped packets. Some implementations insert the timestamp in hardware after the UDP checksum is computed, which breaks the checksum. This experimental RFC defines a checksum complement field to make the checksum right again.

plainLanguage.summary: OWAMP and TWAMP measure network delay by sending test packets that carry a timestamp. This RFC describes how a device that adds the timestamp in hardware can keep the UDP checksum on the packet correct, so that delay measurements stay accurate.

questions: when not to use checksum complement
subtitle: Reserving the last two bytes of a measurement packet so hardware timestamping does not break the UDP checksum.

tldr.problem: OWAMP and TWAMP measure delay with timestamped test packets, and a hardware timestamping engine rewrites the timestamp after the software has already computed the UDP checksum.
tldr.mechanism: The last 2 octets of the packet padding become a Checksum Complement that carries an incremental correction, so a device that changes the timestamp can keep the UDP checksum correct by editing those two bytes.
tldr.outcome: The receiver needs no changes at all: it checks the checksum as usual and treats the two bytes as ordinary padding, so the mechanism works with existing OWAMP and TWAMP implementations.

facts.label: TWAMP minimum padding
facts.value: At least 29 octets unauthenticated, 58 octets authenticated

facts.label: UDP protocols covered
facts.value: OWAMP and TWAMP over IPv4 and over IPv6

today: RFC 7820 is an Experimental RFC that has not been obsoleted or updated, so it still describes the Checksum Complement for OWAMP and TWAMP. The same mechanism is defined for the Network Time Protocol in RFC 7821.

sections.title: The Problem with Hardware Timestamps
sections.content:
The One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (RFC 4656) and the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (RFC 5357) measure delay in IP networks by sending timestamped test packets. Delay and delay variation are often part of a Service Level Agreement, so the measurements have to be accurate.

Accuracy improves when the packet is timestamped in hardware as it leaves the host, rather than later in software. A hardware timestamping engine writes the transmission time into the Timestamp field of every outgoing test packet, while the software layer above it builds and sends the packet.

The trouble is that OWAMP and TWAMP test packets travel over UDP. When any part of the UDP payload changes, the UDP Checksum field has to change with it. When using UDP over IPv4, an entity that cannot update the checksum has no choice except to assign a value of zero to the field, which makes the receiver ignore the checksum and potentially accept corrupted packets. UDP over IPv6 does not allow a zero checksum except in specific cases, and RFC 6936 says that using one is generally not recommended and should be avoided where possible.

Since such an entity changes only one field, the Timestamp field, the UDP checksum can be fixed incrementally rather than recomputed from scratch.
sections.plainLanguage: OWAMP and TWAMP measure network delay by sending test packets that carry a timestamp. This RFC explains how a device that adds the timestamp in hardware can keep the packet's UDP checksum correct, so the delay measurement stays accurate.

sections.title: The Checksum Complement
sections.content:
The Checksum Complement is a 2-octet field piggybacked at the end of the test packet, in the last 2 octets of the UDP payload. OWAMP and TWAMP test packets already contain a Packet Padding field, and this document uses the last 2 octets of that padding for the complement.

The purpose is to compensate for changes made by an intermediate entity. Because only the Timestamp field changes, the UDP checksum can be updated incrementally, using the method set out in RFC 1624. A similar problem is addressed in Annex E of the IEEE 1588 standard, where 2 octets are appended to the Precision Time Protocol payload for UDP checksum updates when that protocol runs over IPv6.

Appendix A of this document works the arithmetic through. The sender's software builds a test packet with timestamp T and UDP checksum U, where U equals a constant, the checksum of all the other covered fields, plus the checksum of T. The timestamping engine then changes T to T' and writes a complement C whose checksum is checksum(T) minus checksum(T'). After that change, U is still the correct checksum of the packet as it leaves the host. The receiver computes the usual UDP checksum and finds U, because the complement sits inside the padding and is included in the computation without special treatment.

The document notes a practical benefit: if packet data is processed in serial order, it is simpler to update the Timestamp field first and then the Checksum Complement, rather than updating the timestamp and then reaching back into the UDP header to update the checksum.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to reserve two bytes at the end of the test packet for a correction value. A device that changes the timestamp also changes those two bytes, which keeps the UDP checksum right without recalculating the whole checksum.

sections.title: Where the Complement Goes in Test Packets
sections.content:
A Checksum Complement MAY be used in OWAMP test packets sent by the sender to the receiver, in TWAMP test packets sent by the sender to the reflector, and in TWAMP test packets sent by the reflector to the sender. The document applies to both OWAMP and TWAMP over IPv4 and over IPv6.

The transmitter of an OWAMP or TWAMP test packet MAY include a Checksum Complement, incorporated in the last 2 octets of the padding. If it does, it MUST include a Packet Padding field long enough to hold the complement, and the length of that padding is negotiated during session initiation through the Padding Length field in the Request-Session or Request-TW-Session message.

  • In OWAMP, the padding length is at least 2 octets, which lets the sender put the complement in the last 2 octets of the padding.
  • In TWAMP, the padding length is at least 29 octets in unauthenticated mode and at least 58 octets in authenticated mode. The extra padding is required because the header of a reflector test packet is longer than the header of a sender test packet, by 27 octets in unauthenticated mode and 56 octets in authenticated mode. The reflector packet therefore has less padding than the sender packet, and the minimum length lets both sides use a 2-octet complement.

If the minimum length requirement is not met, the reflector cannot use a Checksum Complement in the reflected test packets, but the sender can still use one in the test packets it transmits. Two optional TWAMP features, octet reflection and symmetrical size, add a Length of padding to reflect field to the session request, and both length fields must be defined so that the padding expands at least 2 octets beyond the end of the reflected octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Both protocols already have a padding area at the end of their test packets, and the two correction bytes go there. The sender must announce a long enough padding when it starts the session: 2 bytes for OWAMP, and 29 or 58 bytes for TWAMP depending on whether the session is authenticated.

sections.title: Interoperability with Existing Implementations
sections.content:
The document imposes no new requirements on the receiving end of a test packet. The UDP layer at the receiver performs the conventional UDP checksum verification, and the OWAMP or TWAMP layer treats the Checksum Complement as part of the padding.

Because the receiving protocol stack does the normal checksum check, the existence of the complement is transparent to it. That transparency is what allows the mechanism to work with existing implementations that comply with OWAMP or TWAMP.

The document separates the work into two logical layers, a protocol layer and a timestamping layer, and assumes the two are synchronized about whether the complement is enabled. Because both layers reside in the same network device, it assumes no protocol is needed to synchronize them. When the complement is enabled, the protocol layer verifies that test packets include the necessary padding, so the timestamping layer does not have to check this for en-route packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving end does not need to change anything. It checks the UDP checksum as usual and treats the two extra bytes as ordinary padding, so old and new equipment can work together.

sections.title: Authentication and Encryption
sections.content:
Both OWAMP and TWAMP may use authentication or encryption. In authenticated mode the test packets carry an HMAC, a Hashed Message Authentication Code, over some of the fields in the test packet header. The HMAC does not cover the Timestamp field and it does not cover the Packet Padding field.

A Checksum Complement MAY be used when authentication is enabled. Because the HMAC does not cover the timestamp or the padding, an intermediate entity can timestamp test packets and update their Checksum Complement field without modifying the HMAC.

In encrypted mode the Timestamp field is encrypted, and a Checksum Complement SHOULD NOT be used. An intermediate entity that timestamps an encrypted test packet must also re-encrypt it, and re-encryption typically requires storing the packet, re-encrypting it and then forwarding it. The complement therefore has very little value in encrypted mode, since it does not necessarily simplify the implementation. The same reasoning applies when OWAMP or TWAMP is secured by other measures, such as RFC 7717, which derives keys for these protocols with IKEv2.
sections.plainLanguage: With authentication the two correction bytes are fine, because the authentication code does not cover the timestamp or the padding. With encryption they are not worth using, because the device has to decrypt and encrypt the packet anyway.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The scheme is intended for use inside an OWAMP or TWAMP enabled node, to make hardware timestamping engines easier to implement. It is not intended for the intermediate switches and routers between the sender and the receiver or reflector, and any modification of a test packet by those devices should be considered a malicious man-in-the-middle attack.

The document stresses that the scheme does not increase the protocol's vulnerability to such an attack. A man-in-the-middle attacker who modifies a packet and its Checksum Complement is logically in the same position as an attacker who modifies a packet and its UDP Checksum field.

The concept is intended for unauthenticated mode or authenticated mode only. As in the previous section, using the Checksum Complement in encrypted mode does not simplify the implementation compared with the conventional checksum, so it should not be used there.
sections.plainLanguage: The two extra bytes are for the measuring device itself, not for the routers in between. A router that changes a test packet is treated as an attack, and this scheme does not make such an attack easier or harder than editing the ordinary UDP checksum would.

data.title: How the complement keeps the checksum correct

checksum(C) = checksum(T) - checksum(T')
